Two more, quickly. When a cache fills, LRU, least recently used, drops the entry untouched longest: a good default. LFU, least frequently used, keeps popular keys through a quiet spell. First in, first out evicts in insertion order, used or not. And a TTL expires entries on a timer, bounding staleness whatever the memory pressure. Most systems pair LRU with a TTL. And the consistency models to know. Strong: every read reflects the latest write. Eventual: replicas converge once writes stop, and a read can be stale meanwhile. Between them, read-your-writes, the fix from question five, and monotonic reads, where you never see time go backwards. A feed can be eventual; a bank balance usually needs strong.

Question twelve. Design a news feed: fan-out on write, or on read? Fan-out on write, or push, copies each new post's ID into every follower's precomputed feed, so reading one is a cheap lookup. Its cost is per follower: two hundred followers, two hundred writes. A celebrity with fifty million followers makes fifty million writes from one post: a write storm. Fan-out on read, or pull, builds the feed on request from everyone you follow. Posting is cheap, but follow three hundred accounts and every load reads three hundred timelines. Feeds are read far more often than people post, so push usually wins: it does the work once per post, not on every load. So real systems mix them: push for ordinary accounts, pull for celebrities, merged at read time. Follow five celebrities, and a load is six reads, not three hundred, and no post costs fifty million writes. That's the design, grown for ten times the traffic. Every box in it talks to the others through an API. Next: API design.
